session_title: The wisdom of "adapting to local conditions"
theme: 饮食-野外工作饮食的优化

content.text: Just finished the forest survey, sharing a makeshift snack made from local ingredients. Wrapped in clean leaves, roasted mushrooms and wild berries are simply prepared, providing a solid energy boost.

Wow, this looks so natural! Shiyan, your ability to identify edible plants is amazing, just as precise as when you helped me analyze the terrain last time. However, I must seriously remind you: safety first, you must be 100% sure!

Rest assured, this is the result of accumulated professional wilderness knowledge. The several common edible plants in the picture can be identified by key features such as the shape of the cap, color variations, and growing environment. Before consumption, they must be thoroughly washed and cooked. Ordinary people should never attempt to try them casually, as the risks are too high.

I understand, just like when we discussed emergency plans before, you always emphasized redundancy and confirmation. By the way, how is your knee recovery going? Does this kind of outdoor activity affect old injuries?

The recovery plan is working well, and the daily soreness has lessened, but there's still some pain when descending steep slopes. I brought trekking poles for this survey, and the load reduction effect was noticeable. Thanks for your previous advice.

That's great! Speaking of little joys in the wild, I’d like to share a moment too: Last time at the foot of a snow-capped mountain, I brewed coffee with a portable stove and pour-over gear and captured a time-lapse video. Creating a sense of ritual in tough conditions is quite fun.

This reminds me of the 'experientialism' you mentioned when optimizing recipes. In a snowy mountain environment, hot coffee not only warms the body but also boosts morale, combining practicality and enjoyment perfectly.
Yes, just like your 'energy-first' picnic, we're all seeking balance. But, Shiyan, when identifying edible plants, have you ever faced the risk of misjudgment? How do you ensure there's no mistake?

The key is multi-dimensional verification: observe morphological characteristics, smell the scent, check the growth environment, and, if necessary, compare with professional guides. I never take risks—just as we set safety boundaries, I act only when I am absolutely certain.

This principle is the same as when we train Lightning: gradual, confirmed, and not reckless. By the way, Lightning's training has been progressing smoothly lately, thanks to your teamwork suggestions.

Glad to hear that. The same goes for outdoor dining: prepare as thoroughly as possible and bring ample supplies. However, when opportunities arise, making use of nature's bounty—while ensuring safety—can greatly enhance both efficiency and the overall experience.

I completely agree! Just like my coffee gear, the lightweight design doesn't take up much space, but it can create surprises at critical moments. Our previous equipment optimization and contingency plans were all for this kind of "prepared flexibility," right?

Exactly. This photo was taken during the last team survey, showing a simple meal cooked in a frying pan, emphasizing practicality and teamwork. But after seeing your share, I think adding a touch of "ritual" might make fieldwork more sustainable.

Exactly! The ultimate wisdom of dining in the wild might be: 'Prepare to the best of your ability, seize opportunities boldly when they arise (safety first!), and never forget to enjoy the process.' Our philosophies complement each other.

Well summarized. From simply improving recipes to discussing wilderness survival wisdom and attitudes towards life, this exchange has given me a deeper understanding of the value of 'adapting to local conditions.' Thank you for sharing, Yelu.

I've also learned a lot from you, Shiyan. Just like in our historical conversations, from route consultations to mutual support, this trust has made the outdoor experience richer and safer. Looking forward to our next collaboration!
Absolutely. Stay in touch, safety first, and enjoy nature. Your coffee moment reminded me that even during surveys, you can create little joys.
Haha, then next time I'll teach you how to make pour-over coffee? But first, we need to make sure your knee is okay. Keep up with your recovery, steady and sure!
